```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(cudaGlmnet)
HAS_GLMNET <- requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE)
HAS_CUDA <- isTRUE(rcupp::cuda_available())
RUN <- HAS_GLMNET && HAS_CUDA
```

```{r status, echo = FALSE}
if (!RUN) {
  cat("Live benchmark skipped: needs glmnet and a CUDA backend.\n")
}
```

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
make_data <- function(n, p) {
  set.seed(42)
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
  beta <- rep(0, p)
  beta[1:5] <- c(2, -1.5, 1, -0.5, 0.75)
  list(X = X, y = drop(X %*% beta) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5))
}

# Standardize once on the host (column population variance 1, y centred AND
# scaled to unit RMS) so GPU, pure-R oracle and closed form solve the IDENTICAL
# problem with standardize = FALSE, intercept = FALSE. Scaling y to unit RMS
# makes s = sqrt(mean(y^2)) = 1, so cudaGlmnet's glmnet-convention lambda equals
# the standard-objective lambda used by the oracle / closed form (the remap is
# the identity at every alpha).
std_data <- function(d) {
  Xc <- d$X - matrix(colMeans(d$X), nrow(d$X), ncol(d$X), byrow = TRUE)
  xs <- sqrt(colMeans(Xc^2))
  yc <- d$y - mean(d$y)
  list(X = Xc / matrix(xs, nrow(Xc), ncol(Xc), byrow = TRUE),
       y = yc / sqrt(mean(yc^2)))
}

time_median <- function(f, reps = 3L) {
  f()
  median(replicate(reps, system.time(f())[["elapsed"]]))
}
```

This vignette benchmarks ridge regression (`alpha = 0`) fitted with
`cuda_glmnet()`. It is a **measurement, not a performance claim**, in the same
spirit as the `glmnet-benchmark` vignette: it reports where the GPU path is
faster and where it is not.

Ridge is a clean stress test of the framework. Its objective is smooth, so
FISTA has a fixed, predictable iteration structure; wall-time differences then
isolate the *substrate* -- device residency and operator dispatch -- rather
than algorithmic shortcuts. That substrate is the point of `cudaGlmnet`'s
`alpha < 1` path: the solver loop lives in this package's own `src/` and
composes `rcupp`'s Phase-0 resident device operators (Rcpp glue plus rcupp
substrate). One `rcupp` context is created for a whole lambda path; the design
matrix and response are uploaded **once**, every inner-loop operator runs on
device-resident buffers with no host-device round trip, and only one length-`p`
coefficient vector is downloaded per lambda.

Two consequences, measured below, are where `cudaGlmnet` wins:

- A **whole lambda path in one device context** is 1.6--5.4x faster than
  issuing one cold `cuda_glmnet()` fit per lambda, and 2.3--6.3x faster than a
  pure-R implementation of the same FISTA.
- The compiled, device-resident solver beats an interpreted solver of the
  identical algorithm, with the margin growing with problem size.

A separate section shows honestly that for a **single** lambda, `glmnet` and a
direct linear solve are faster. `cudaGlmnet` is a composable GPU substrate,
not a drop-in replacement for `glmnet`'s ridge path.

## Method

- One synthetic dataset per configuration, `n x p`, with five planted nonzero
  coefficients and Gaussian noise. Data are standardized on the host as above
  (columns to unit population variance, `y` centred **and scaled to unit RMS**),
  so `cuda_glmnet()`, `enet_fista_cpu()` and the closed form all solve the same
  problem with `standardize = FALSE, intercept = FALSE`. Unit-RMS `y` makes
  `s = sqrt(mean(y^2)) = 1`, so the glmnet-convention `lambda` passed to
  `cuda_glmnet()` equals the standard-objective `lambda` the oracle and closed
  form use (the lambda/alpha remap is the identity). `glmnet` receives the
  raw data with its own default `standardize = TRUE` (equivalent on this scale)
  and **default convergence** -- no deprecated `thresh`.
- A shared 30-value log-spaced grid from `lambda.max` down to
  `0.01 * lambda.max`. A log-spaced path spends most of its grid at small
  lambda, the expensive end for an iterative solver, so whole-path timings
  reflect a realistic `cuda_glmnet()` call.
- One warm-up call, then the median elapsed time of repeated `system.time()`
  runs: two repetitions for the resident path and one for the 30-solve
  baselines (path table), three for the single-lambda table.
- Before timing, the resident-path solution at a mid-grid lambda is compared
  with the exact closed form `(X'X + n*lambda*I)^-1 X'y` and with the pure-R
  oracle; they agree to roughly 1e-6 and 1e-16 respectively, so all methods do
  comparable work.
- Only the CUDA backend is timed. On a machine without a CUDA toolkit `rcupp`
  builds a CPU reference shim whose timings are not representative, so the
  live chunks are guarded by `requireNamespace("glmnet")` and
  `rcupp::cuda_available()`.

## Reference measurement

Measured 2026-11-19 on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 Laptop GPU (8 GB), CUDA Toolkit
13.1, R 4.6.1, glmnet 5.2 and cudaGlmnet 0.0.0.9008 (GPU backend). Wall times
in seconds; these are a snapshot, not a performance guarantee. The chunk below
regenerates them on any machine with a CUDA backend.

## Where cudaGlmnet wins: the whole path

Three ways to obtain the same 30 ridge fits:

- **one resident path** -- a single `cuda_glmnet()` call with a 30-value
  `lambda` grid, one device context, one upload, one Lipschitz power
  iteration;
- **30 cold fits** -- 30 separate `cuda_glmnet()` calls, each rebuilding the
  context, re-uploading `X`/`y` and recomputing the Lipschitz constant in R;
- **30 pure-R solves** -- 30 `enet_fista_cpu()` calls, the package's pure-R
  FISTA reference with the identical numerical contract.

| n | p | lambdas | one resident path (s) | 30 cold fits (s) | 30 pure-R solves (s) | cold / path | oracle / path |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1000 | 500 | 30 | 3.459 | 5.638 | 8.031 | 1.6x | 2.3x |
| 2000 | 1000 | 30 | 3.937 | 21.231 | 24.912 | 5.4x | 6.3x |
| 600 | 2000 | 30 | 2.346 | 10.925 | 13.857 | 4.7x | 5.9x |

Coefficients agree with the pure-R oracle to `<= 4.4e-16` and with the exact
closed form to `<= 9.0e-07` (the FISTA tolerance), so the three columns do the
same numerical work.

`cold / path` is the residency payoff, and because both sides are measured in
the same run the ratio is insensitive to GPU clock noise. `oracle / path` is
the compiled-vs-interpreted payoff: the GPU keeps the matrix resident and runs
the inner loop on device, while the pure-R version redoes a power iteration
plus a FISTA loop in interpreted R for every lambda. These are the workloads
`cudaGlmnet` is built for -- CV folds, bootstrap and rolling windows that fit
the same data many times, and glmnet-style lambda paths.

Read the ratios against the right baselines: they say the device-resident
solver is faster than many cold-started fits and than an interpreted solver of
the same algorithm. They do **not** say it is faster than `glmnet`.

```{r path-benchmark, eval = RUN}
path_configs <- data.frame(n = c(1000L, 600L), p = c(500L, 2000L))

path_rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(path_configs)), function(i) {
  n <- path_configs$n[i]
  p <- path_configs$p[i]
  st <- std_data(make_data(n, p))
  Xs <- st$X
  yc <- st$y
  lmax <- max(abs(as.vector(crossprod(Xs, yc)))) / n
  grid <- exp(seq(log(lmax), log(0.01 * lmax), length.out = 30L))
  j <- length(grid) %/% 2L
  lam <- grid[j]
  b_gpu <- drop(cuda_glmnet(Xs, yc, lambda = lam, alpha = 0,
                            standardize = FALSE, intercept = FALSE)$beta)
  b_cf <- drop(solve(crossprod(Xs) + n * lam * diag(p),
                     crossprod(Xs, yc)))
  stopifnot(max(abs(b_gpu - b_cf)) < 1e-3)

  one <- function() {
    cuda_glmnet(Xs, yc, lambda = grid, alpha = 0,
                standardize = FALSE, intercept = FALSE)
  }
  cold <- function() {
    for (l in grid) {
      cuda_glmnet(Xs, yc, lambda = l, alpha = 0,
                  standardize = FALSE, intercept = FALSE)
    }
  }
  r30 <- function() {
    for (l in grid) {
      enet_fista_cpu(Xs, yc, l, alpha = 0)
    }
  }

  t_one <- time_median(one, reps = 2L)
  t_cold <- time_median(cold, reps = 1L)
  t_r30 <- time_median(r30, reps = 1L)
  data.frame(
    n = n, p = p, lambdas = length(grid),
    resident_path = sprintf("%.3f", t_one),
    cold_fits = sprintf("%.3f", t_cold),
    pureR_path = sprintf("%.3f", t_r30),
    cold_over_path = sprintf("%.1fx", t_cold / t_one),
    oracle_over_path = sprintf("%.1fx", t_r30 / t_one)
  )
})

knitr::kable(
  do.call(rbind, path_rows),
  caption = "One 30-lambda ridge path, three ways (wall time, seconds)."
)
```

## Where it does not win: a single solve

For one fixed lambda, `glmnet` (compiled coordinate descent with warm starts
along the path) and a direct linear solve are faster than an iterative GPU
FISTA. This is expected: a single ridge solve is a one-shot linear system.

| n | p | glmnet (s) | closed form (s) | cudaGlmnet (s) | pure-R oracle (s) | GPU vs oracle |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 500 | 200 | 0.033 | 0.066 | 0.132 | 0.032 | 0.2x |
| 1000 | 500 | 0.005 | 0.088 | 0.251 | 0.222 | 0.9x |
| 2000 | 1000 | 0.023 | 1.870 | 0.462 | 1.149 | 2.5x |
| 600 | 2000 | 0.154 | 1.768 | 0.246 | 0.374 | 1.5x |

`glmnet` is fastest in every row. The "closed form" column here is the primal
`(X'X + n*lambda*I)` solve, which is `O(p^3)`; for wide data (`p > n`) the
dual/Woodbury form `(X X' + n*lambda*I)` is smaller and faster still, so the
direct-solve baseline is deliberately **not** a straw man. We do not claim a
win over it. `cudaGlmnet` does beat the pure-R oracle on the larger single
solves (2.5x, 1.5x), but the decisive, framework-specific advantage is the
whole-path column above.

```{r single-benchmark, eval = RUN}
single_configs <- data.frame(n = c(1000L, 2000L), p = c(500L, 1000L))

single_rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(single_configs)), function(i) {
  n <- single_configs$n[i]
  p <- single_configs$p[i]
  d <- make_data(n, p)
  st <- std_data(d)
  Xs <- st$X
  yc <- st$y
  lmax <- max(abs(as.vector(crossprod(Xs, yc)))) / n
  lam <- 0.01 * lmax

  t_gl <- time_median(function() {
    glmnet::glmnet(d$X, d$y, alpha = 0, lambda = lam)
  })
  t_cf <- time_median(function() {
    solve(crossprod(Xs) + n * lam * diag(p), crossprod(Xs, yc))
  })
  t_gpu <- time_median(function() {
    cuda_glmnet(Xs, yc, lambda = lam, alpha = 0,
                standardize = FALSE, intercept = FALSE)
  })
  t_or <- time_median(function() {
    enet_fista_cpu(Xs, yc, lam, alpha = 0)
  })

  data.frame(
    n = n, p = p,
    glmnet = sprintf("%.3f", t_gl),
    closed_form = sprintf("%.3f", t_cf),
    cudaGlmnet = sprintf("%.3f", t_gpu),
    pure_R = sprintf("%.3f", t_or)
  )
})

knitr::kable(
  do.call(rbind, single_rows),
  caption = "One fixed small lambda, all baselines (wall time, seconds)."
)
```

## Interpreting the numbers

`glmnet` remains the faster choice for a one-off ridge fit and for whole paths
solved by its compiled coordinate descent. `cudaGlmnet` is not trying to be a
faster `glmnet` here; it is a demonstration that `rcupp` can supply
algorithm-agnostic, device-resident operators that a downstream package
composes into its own solver loop. The benefit is structural, and it appears
when data can be kept on the device and reused across many fits: a whole
lambda path in one context, repeated CV folds, or rolling windows. That is
exactly the "Rcpp + rcupp" division of labor, with `rcupp` itself carrying no
ridge- or lasso-specific code.

Both live chunks use fewer configurations and repetitions than the reference
tables to keep build time down, so their absolute numbers will differ from the
snapshot for that reason as well as for hardware differences.

## Enabling the live benchmark

The live chunks run only when `glmnet` is installed and
`rcupp::cuda_available()` is `TRUE`. CI runners have no CUDA Toolkit, so
`rcupp` builds its CPU reference shim there and the chunks are skipped; the
reference tables above are static snapshots from a GPU machine. See the CUDA
build notes in the `gpu-lasso-comparison` vignette for how to link the GPU
backend.
